 Follow Mathematicians find an infinite number of Ramanujan equations
 Knots show how to generate infinitely many formulas of a kind developed by the visionary genius
 Lyndie Chiou Thu, October 29, 2026 at 10:30 AM UTC 8 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. The legendary mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan and Yifeng Huang, a postdoctoral researcher at Emory University, have something in common: they will not be ignored. In 1912 Ramanujan, a 24-year-old clerk at what was then the Madras Port Trust in India, began mailing pages of new, unproven formulas to mathematicians across England. One of his letters eventually reached British mathematician G. H. Hardy at the University of Cambridge, who recognized Ramanujan as a visionary, invited him to visit and helped launch his groundbreaking career .
 More than a century later, Huang, while a graduate student at the University of Michigan, began e-mailing mathematicians letter after letter—more than 40 in total. He scarcely heard back.
 Huang's ideas concerned two formulas that appeared in Ramanujan's letters and are now known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. In September 2026 Huang and a few collaborators uploaded a proof that the historic equations represent a single case of a much grander geometrical theory. In particular, the work showed that the Roger-Ramanujan identities correspond to a trefoil knot in a certain space. The trefoil, known as the shape of the familiar Celtic knot, is one of the simplest mathematical knots. And related knots, they found, reveal an infinite number of previously unknown identities.

 "Everything about this subject, even the original discovery, is a surprise," says George Andrews, a mathematician at Pennsylvania State University and an expert on Ramanujan's math. Ramanujan, Hardy and their collaborators "were all unable to prove this," he adds. "So the things that have cropped up from knot theory were a total surprise to me."
 The Roger-Ramanujan Identities 
 Hardy was responsible for shaping much of early 20th century number theory. Initially skeptical when he received a letter from Ramanujan, Hardy later wrote that he recognized the letter's author as "a mathematician of the highest quality, a man of altogether exceptional originality and power." It was a pivotal moment .
 Two of Ramanujan's formulas were startling: they represented an infinite series of sums on one side and an infinite series of products on the other, with no visible reason for the two to agree. By 1916 British mathematician Percy MacMahon had found a way to read them. These two equations were similar to ones studied two centuries earlier by mathematician Leonhard Euler. Euler had a neat trick for sidestepping such complexity: he connected the equations to a type of counting problem known as a "partition." A partition of a number is a way of writing it as a sum. MacMahon transformed Ramanujan's formulas into two kinds of partitions that looked nothing alike, but whose counts always came out identical.
 Advertisement Advertisement Here's how one side of a Ramanujan equation was partitioned: count the number of ways to sum up to a certain value using numbers that are at least two whole numbers apart. For instance, 6 can be written as 1 + 5, 2 + 4 and 6. So there are three partitions.
 On the other side, sum using only numbers that end in 1, 4, 6 or 9. For 6, the answer is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 4 and 6, which also gives three partitions.
 The formulas say these two very different counts agree for every number. Before Ramanujan could prove them, he came across an obscure proof by English mathematician Leonard James Rogers in an old math journal. Thus, the equations became known as the Rogers-Ramanujan identities.
 "It was regarded, for most of the 20th century, as an isolated gem," Andrews says. No one suspected it lay at the heart of a much larger theory.
 Advertisement Advertisement In the early 1970s Andrews uncovered an infinite family of the identities. "I discovered them only to learn that [mathematician] Basil Gordon had done them first," Andrews says, "which was a huge disappointment for me."
 The new family came to be known as the Andrews-Gordon identities.
 Since then the identities have turned up in strange places: in representation theory, in the study of symmetric functions, even in physics via the "hard hexagon model," which describes how gas atoms can settle onto a surface in a triangular pattern.
 "Who would have thought that the Rogers-Ramanujan identities were related to how liquid helium behaves when poured onto a graphite plate?" Andrews says.
 A Pinch to Build a Conjecture 
 Yifeng Huang had a hunch.
 Advertisement Advertisement Matrices—little spreadsheets of numbers—can undergo operations such as flips and transpositions, which must be done in a certain order to get the correct result. But if the values of the matrices are chosen such that the order of operations doesn't matter (meaning they "commute"), then the matrices behave like coordinates and can be used to describe curves. Take any smooth curve, such as the parabola y = x 2 , and replace y and x with pairs of matrices. A textbook-level problem might ask: How many pairs of matrices make the equation true? A math student can find the answer.
 But what happens if you use a curve that isn't so smooth—one that has a "pinch" in it, also known as a singularity? Now textbook theory breaks down. These matrix counts had neverbeen studied.
 While he was still a Ph.D. student at the University of Michigan, Huang started counting matrices on pinched curves such as y 2 = x 3 , which comes to a sharp tip when x and y equal 0. Before long, his counts reproduced a familiar formula: one side of the Rogers-Ramanujan identities. "Already this discovery is fascinating," Huang says. "I'm wondering what is going on. It can't be a coincidence."
 From that single example, Huang made a bold, vague guess: What if every pinched curve hid a new identity, with its matrix count collapsing into a neat formula? Hoping to discuss the idea further, Huang wrote letters to a small group of mathematicians—around five to 10 people.
 Advertisement Advertisement University of Virginia mathematician Ken Ono received one of those letters. But thinking Huang's idea was "crazy," Ono dismissed it.
 Another letter recipient was Alexei Oblomkov, a mathematician at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, whose work connects algebraic geometry and knot theory. "I thought it was kind of a great idea, and later we met at one of the conferences, and I liked the idea even more," Oblomkov says.
 By then, Huang and Ruofan Jiang, now a mathematician at the University of California, Berkeley, had devised a systematic way to count how many matrices make the formulas for pinched curves true.
 Oblomkov brought geometry to the table. Zoom in on the pinch in y 2 = x 3 , he advised, and surround it with a tiny sphere in four dimensions, where mathematicians say such curves naturally live. The curve pierces the sphere along a closed loop in a "trefoil" knot. Both counts lead to the classic Rogers-Ramanujan identities. What about another curve? It also led to another knot, which was hiding another family of identities. And another curve led to yet more.
 Advertisement Advertisement The team's ideas crystalized into the Huang-Jiang-Oblomkov (HJO) conjecture. Simply stated, pick any two numbers a and b that are greater than 1, with no common factor. The conjecture predicts that for the curve x a = y b , a count of the matrix solutions will always collapse into a Rogers-Ramanujan-type identity. This translates into infinitely many families of identities, one for every value of a . The case a = 2 is the family Andrews and Gordon found. Every larger value of a was uncharted. And each curve comes with its own knot: the trefoil for a = 2 and b = 3 and more intricately wound torus knots for the rest.
 The Proof 
 Again, Huang began sending out e-mails—more than 40 in 2023—and gave a circuit of seminar talks.
 This time, when Ono received one of Huang's letters, he found the idea "mind-blowing," he says. "That's when I joined this chase."
 By then Ono had signed on to the artificial intelligence company Axiom Math as its founding mathematician. He, Huang and another Axiom mathematician, Kenny Lau, worked for seven months in tandem with AxiomProver, the company's math-focused AI system.
 Advertisement Advertisement Because the ideas were so new, Ono says, they couldn't simply ask an AI model to solve the problem—there was no literature for it to learn from. Instead AxiomProver worked like a research assistant, testing a far more expansive space of ideas than would be humanly possible. It also translated the proof into Lean, a machine-friendly language for automated proof checking. In the end, the quartet made of humans and AI stitched together ideas from five different areas of math to prove the conjecture.
 Ono's take on AI in math is more hopeful than many in his field. "Everyone talks about the end of math ," he says. "But someone had to invent this structure. This is what we should be doing."
 The team members posted their HJO conjecture to the preprint server arXiv.org in August 2026. And in September, the three followed up with the conjecture's proof .
 Recast as geometry, the old identities now point toward unmapped territory, raising questions that mathematicians are eager to explore.
 Advertisement Advertisement "We found something exciting," Oblomkov says, "a way to extend the geometry in the case when it's not a trefoil knot, but a so-called Hopf link—basically you have two circles tied together. So that will be the next paper."
 Oblomkov also says Fields Medalist Peter Scholze has published a few papers that take some of Huang's ideas even further. The pinched curves x a = y b are only the beginning. The equation is, Huang says, "only the first example of a singularity I would write down." Oblomkov agrees: "It's just the first case, and there will be many more."
